title: Green Nanotechnology-Based Zinc Oxide Nanomaterials for Biomedical Applications: Synthesis, Properties, Therapeutic Utility, and Translational Perspectives

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Green ZnO Nanomaterials for Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Zinc oxide nanomaterials: core physicochemical features
subsections.content:
Zinc oxide is a II–VI semiconductor whose nanomaterial appeal originates from the coexistence of electronic, surface, and structural functionalities within a single platform. In its thermodynamically stable wurtzite phase, ZnO exhibits a direct wide band gap of about 3.37 eV and a large exciton binding energy of approximately 60 meV, enabling efficient near-UV absorption, room-temperature excitonic behavior, and optoelectronic responsiveness that are relevant to imaging, sensing, and photoactivated therapy ref [1]. At the nanoscale, these properties become strongly shape- and defect-dependent, with rods, wires, spheres, flowers, and hierarchical architectures displaying distinct surface energies and charge-transport characteristics.

A second defining feature is the high density of chemically active surfaces and intrinsic defects, including oxygen vacancies, zinc interstitials, and surface hydroxyl groups. These features influence colloidal stability, adsorption of biomolecules, dissolution into Zn2+, and the generation of reactive oxygen species under dark or irradiated conditions ref [2]. Such defect-mediated reactivity is central to many biological effects of ZnO, including antimicrobial action and selective cytotoxicity, but it also means that particle size, crystallinity, and surface functionalization critically govern biocompatibility.

ZnO nanomaterials are also notable for piezoelectricity and polar surfaces associated with the non-centrosymmetric wurtzite lattice. Nanoscale deformation can induce surface polarization, while the Zn-terminated and O-terminated crystal faces provide anisotropic growth and differential protein interactions ref [3]. In physiological media, these characteristics combine with moderate biodegradability to produce a dynamically transforming nanomaterial whose performance reflects an interplay among morphology, defects, surface chemistry, and local pH ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Green ZnO Nanomaterials for Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Green nanotechnology as a paradigm in nanomedicine
subsections.content:
Green nanotechnology has emerged as a guiding paradigm in nanomedicine because it links material innovation with principles of safer chemistry, reduced waste, and life-cycle awareness. Rather than treating synthesis merely as a technical step, this framework emphasizes renewable feedstocks, benign solvents, lower energy inputs, and intrinsic biocompatibility as design criteria that can shape downstream biological performance. Foundational discussions of green chemistry and sustainable nanoscience argue that hazard prevention should be built into nanomaterial development from the outset, not addressed only after biomedical translation challenges appear ref [5], ref [6].

In practical nanomedicine, this paradigm has encouraged the use of plant extracts, polysaccharides, proteins, and microorganisms as reducing, stabilizing, or structure-directing agents. Such routes can diminish reliance on harsh reagents while simultaneously introducing surface chemistries that influence colloidal stability, protein corona formation, cellular uptake, and immunological response. The concept therefore extends beyond eco-friendly synthesis to a broader "safety-by-design" strategy, in which physicochemical control and toxicological foresight are integrated early in material development ref [7], ref [8].

For ZnO-based systems, green nanotechnology is especially relevant because biomedical utility depends not only on nanoscale architecture but also on residual impurities, defect chemistry, dissolution behavior, and surface-bound biomolecules inherited from synthesis. A green paradigm thus provides a coherent framework for evaluating ZnO nanomaterials as multifunctional biomedical platforms whose therapeutic promise should be balanced with reproducibility, biosafety, and environmental responsibility across the translational pipeline ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Green ZnO Nanomaterials for Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Why ZnO is attractive for biomedical applications
subsections.content:
ZnO is attractive for biomedicine because it combines multifunctional physicochemical behavior with relatively simple composition and scalable manufacture. As a wide-band-gap semiconductor, ZnO exhibits size- and defect-dependent optical responses, including strong UV absorption, photoluminescence, and reactive oxygen species generation under irradiation, features that are useful for imaging, antimicrobial action, and photoactivated therapy ref [10], ref [11]. Its nanostructures can also be prepared in diverse morphologies—particles, rods, wires, flowers, and porous assemblies—allowing control over surface area, cellular interactions, and payload loading.

A second advantage is its biological relevance. Zinc is an essential trace element, and ZnO can undergo pH-responsive dissolution to release Zn2+, which links the material to enzyme function, cell signaling, and antimicrobial effects while also enabling stimulus-responsive therapeutic design ref [12]. This dissolution behavior is especially important in acidic microenvironments, where enhanced ion release and oxidative stress can be exploited against bacteria or tumor cells, although these same mechanisms require careful dose and surface engineering to manage safety ref [13].

ZnO is also compelling because one material platform can support multiple biomedical modalities. It has been explored for antibacterial coatings, drug delivery, biosensing, bioimaging, and tissue engineering, with particularly strong interest in wound healing and bone-related applications where zinc-associated bioactivity may complement structural or antimicrobial functions ref [14]. This breadth of utility makes ZnO a natural candidate for green synthesis strategies aimed at uniting performance, cost-effectiveness, and translational practicality.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Green ZnO Nanomaterials for Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Convergence of sustainability and biomedical performance
subsections.content:
The convergence of sustainability and biomedical performance in ZnO nanomaterials is not merely procedural; it is increasingly understood as a structure–function problem in which the synthetic route shapes clinically relevant behavior. Green fabrication strategies can reduce hazardous reagents and energy demand while simultaneously introducing phytochemical or biopolymer capping layers that alter nucleation, crystal growth, surface charge, colloidal stability, and interfacial bioactivity. This is especially important for ZnO, whose antimicrobial, anticancer, and regenerative effects are highly sensitive to particle size, defect chemistry, dissolution kinetics, and reactive oxygen species generation ref [15], ref [16].

From a biomedical perspective, eco-friendly synthesis may therefore serve as a design lever rather than a simple sustainability label. Plant-derived metabolites, proteins, polysaccharides, and other benign reducing/stabilizing agents can improve dispersion and biocompatibility, and in some cases impart synergistic antioxidant or antimicrobial functionality at the nano–bio interface ref [17]. More broadly, green nanotechnology has been framed as a route to materials whose life-cycle considerations, safer inputs, and functional performance are integrated from the outset, aligning with emerging safe-by-design thinking for translational nanomedicine ref [6].

For green-synthesized ZnO systems, the key challenge is to move from qualitative claims of “eco-friendliness” to quantitative evidence linking sustainable processing with reproducible biomedical outcomes. This requires standardized reporting of precursor origin, extract composition, purification, and batch-to-batch variability, together with rigorous evaluation of efficacy and toxicology. In this sense, sustainability and performance should be treated as co-optimization targets, not competing objectives, in the development of ZnO nanoplatforms for medicine.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Green ZnO Nanomaterials for Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Scope and classification of green-synthesized ZnO systems
subsections.content:
The scope of green-synthesized ZnO systems in biomedicine extends beyond a simple "plant-made nanoparticle" category to a broader family of materials defined by renewable precursors, low-hazard reaction media, and biologically derived structure-directing agents. In practice, these systems include colloidal nanoparticles, nanorods, nanoflowers, hierarchical aggregates, and hybrid surfaces or coatings obtained through extracts, biopolymers, or microbial metabolism under comparatively mild conditions. Reviews of green routes to ZnO emphasize that the biological source is not merely a solvent substitute; it also influences nucleation, crystal growth, surface chemistry, dispersibility, and thus downstream biointeractions ref [18], ref [10].

A useful classification can therefore be organized along three axes. First is the biosynthetic source: plant extract-mediated systems, microorganism-mediated systems, and biotemplate/biopolymer-assisted systems such as starch-, cellulose-, chitosan-, or protein-enabled ZnO ref [18], ref [19]. Second is material architecture: zero-dimensional nanoparticles, one-dimensional wires or rods, two-dimensional films, and three-dimensional hierarchical assemblies, each associated with distinct dissolution, ROS generation, mechanical integration, and cargo-loading behavior. Third is functional intent, separating intrinsically active ZnO for antimicrobial or anticancer action from composite platforms designed for imaging, wound dressings, scaffolds, or controlled drug delivery ref [10], ref [4].

This classification is important because "green synthesis" does not guarantee equivalent biomedical performance or safety. Variability in extract composition, residual phytochemicals, defect density, and corona-forming surface groups can produce substantial differences in cytocompatibility, antimicrobial potency, and degradation behavior. Accordingly, recent green ZnO literature increasingly treats synthesis route, morphology, and intended use as interdependent design variables rather than separate descriptors, supporting a more application-oriented taxonomy for translational nanomedicine ref [19], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Plant-mediated synthesis of ZnO nanoparticles
subsections.content:
Plant-mediated synthesis has emerged as one of the most accessible green routes for producing ZnO nanoparticles because plant extracts simultaneously provide reducing, complexing, and capping functions without the need for hazardous organic solvents or strongly toxic reagents. In a typical protocol, a zinc salt precursor is mixed with an aqueous extract prepared from leaves, peels, seeds, flowers, or latex, followed by pH adjustment and mild heating or calcination to yield crystalline ZnO. This strategy is attractive for biomedical nanomaterials because it can lower synthetic complexity while introducing a phytochemical corona that influences colloidal stability and interfacial behavior ref [17], ref [9].

The chemistry of plant-mediated ZnO formation is strongly linked to extract composition. Polyphenols, flavonoids, sugars, proteins, and organic acids can chelate Zn2+, regulate nucleation, and suppress uncontrolled particle growth, thereby affecting size and morphology. Experimental studies using different botanical sources have reported spherical, quasi-spherical, and rod-like ZnO nanostructures, with antibacterial activity often attributed to the combined effects of nanoscale ZnO and residual bioactive surface moieties ref [9], ref [15]. Work using Vitex negundo leaf extract, for example, demonstrated that a simple plant-assisted process can generate ZnO nanoparticles with measurable antimicrobial performance, illustrating the practical compatibility of this route with biologically oriented applications ref [20].

Despite these advantages, plant-mediated synthesis remains sensitive to seasonal variation, extraction conditions, precursor concentration, and post-synthesis annealing, all of which can alter crystallinity, defect density, and reproducibility. Consequently, the major value of this approach lies not only in its sustainability profile, but also in its tunability: careful standardization of botanical source and processing parameters is essential if plant-derived ZnO is to progress from proof-of-concept synthesis toward reliable biomedical manufacturing ref [17], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Microbial and biotemplate-assisted synthesis
subsections.content:
Microbial synthesis offers a biologically programmed route to ZnO formation in which bacteria, fungi, and yeast supply enzymes, proteins, polysaccharides, and redox-active metabolites that mediate Zn2+ binding, hydrolysis, and subsequent nucleation. Compared with plant extracts, microbial systems can provide better control over metabolite composition through defined culture conditions, although product heterogeneity remains sensitive to strain identity and growth phase. Reviews of biologically mediated nanomaterial synthesis have emphasized that extracellular secretion and cell-surface functional groups can both act as nanoreactors, while ZnO-focused overviews note the relevance of these mechanisms to biocompatible and antimicrobial formulations for biomedical use ref [17], ref [10].

Beyond whole-cell systems, biotemplate-assisted synthesis exploits structurally organized biological matrices to direct ZnO growth. A notable example is the use of S-layer protein lattices as ordered templates for mineral deposition, enabling spatially patterned ZnO nanostructures under mild processing conditions ref [21]. Such templates can constrain crystal orientation and particle packing, whereas softer biomacromolecular scaffolds may favor smaller crystallites with higher defect density and larger specific surface area. These features are attractive for drug loading, biointerfacing, and antimicrobial performance, but they also make purification and batch-to-batch standardization more challenging.

Current work therefore treats microbial and biotemplate routes not simply as greener substitutes for chemical precipitation, but as morphology-engineering platforms. Key design variables include precursor concentration, pH, aeration, incubation time, and the nature of secreted biomolecules or template architectures, all of which strongly influence ZnO phase purity, aggregation state, and surface corona composition ref [10], ref [18]. For translation, the main challenge is to preserve the synthetic advantages of biological mediation while improving reproducibility, biosafety assessment, and scalable downstream processing.

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Phytochemical roles in nanoparticle formation
subsections.content:
In plant-mediated ZnO synthesis, phytochemicals function as a coupled redox, complexation, and passivation system rather than as passive additives. Polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, proteins, and reducing sugars can chelate Zn2+ through hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, and amine groups, thereby modulating precursor hydrolysis and the nucleation density of Zn-containing intermediates. During subsequent dehydration or calcination, these coordinated species are converted to ZnO while residual organics can remain adsorbed on the surface, influencing colloidal stability and biological identity of the nanomaterial ref [9], ref [18].

The balance between reducing strength and capping ability is especially important for controlling crystal growth. Phenolic and carboxylate-rich extracts tend to suppress agglomeration by lowering surface energy and sterically hindering particle coalescence, often yielding smaller particles with higher effective surface area. Spectroscopic studies in green nanomaterial synthesis consistently implicate O-H, C=O, and N-H containing biomolecules in binding and stabilization, supporting a mechanism in which extract composition governs anisotropic growth, defect density, and the accessibility of reactive ZnO facets ref [17], ref [6].

Because plant extracts are chemically heterogeneous, phytochemical variability is also a major source of batch-to-batch differences in ZnO morphology and function. Species, plant part, harvest season, and extraction solvent alter the relative abundance of tannins, flavonoids, and polysaccharides, which in turn changes nucleation kinetics and the extent of organic surface functionalization. This variability helps explain why nominally similar green protocols can produce distinct particle sizes, shapes, and antimicrobial performance, underscoring the need for phytochemical profiling when correlating synthesis conditions with biomedical outcomes ref [18], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Reaction parameters and nanostructure tuning
subsections.content:
In green ZnO synthesis, nanostructure is highly sensitive to reaction chemistry rather than merely to precursor identity. pH is especially influential because it controls zinc hydrolysis, complexation, and the deprotonation state of phytochemicals that act as reducing, chelating, and capping agents. Alkaline conditions generally accelerate nucleation through Zn(OH)2 and related intermediates, often yielding smaller particles, whereas lower pH can slow condensation and favor aggregation or irregular growth. Temperature and reaction time then determine the balance between rapid nucleation and subsequent Ostwald ripening, with higher temperatures usually improving crystallinity but also increasing particle coarsening if capping is insufficient ref [1], ref [15].

Precursor concentration, extract-to-salt ratio, and mixing regime further tune anisotropy and dispersity. Excess zinc ions can outstrip the stabilizing capacity of biomolecules, promoting secondary growth and broad size distributions, while higher extract content often increases surface passivation and limits agglomeration. Such effects are consistent with broader ZnO growth studies showing that supersaturation, hydroxide availability, and adsorption of organic species on specific crystal facets govern the emergence of rods, flowers, spheres, or sheet-like assemblies ref [22], ref [23]. In hydrothermal and solution-based routes, even modest adjustments in solvent composition or aging conditions can shift growth along the polar c-axis, producing marked morphological transitions ref [23].

For biomedical deployment, parameter optimization must therefore target not only size and shape but also colloidal stability, defect density, and residual surface chemistry. Standardized reporting of pH, thermal history, precursor stoichiometry, and extract composition is essential because these variables directly affect reproducibility, dissolution behavior, and downstream bioactivity of green-synthesized ZnO ref [15], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Morphological diversity in green ZnO nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green synthesis yields an unusually broad morphological spectrum of ZnO, including quasi-spherical nanoparticles, rods, flowers, sheets, and hierarchical aggregates. This diversity arises because biogenic media contain multiple ligands, redox-active metabolites, and macromolecular capping species that adsorb selectively on growing crystal faces, thereby altering anisotropic growth along the c-axis and the assembly of primary nuclei into secondary architectures. In ZnO, such shape evolution is especially sensitive to the balance between nucleation rate and facet-specific stabilization, which has long been recognized as a central determinant of nanostructure formation in solution-based routes ref [22], ref [1].

In green systems, plant polyphenols, proteins, polysaccharides, and amino-containing biomolecules can simultaneously complex Zn2+, mediate hydrolysis, and cap emerging nuclei, often producing morphologies that differ from those obtained in simpler chemical baths. Reports using plant extracts have described predominantly spherical and weakly aggregated ZnO at lower precursor or extract concentrations, whereas stronger alkalinity, longer aging, or post-calcination commonly promote rods, hexagonal crystallites, and flower-like assemblies with higher crystallinity and exposed polar surfaces ref [19], ref [20]. Biotemplate-guided methods further expand this landscape by using organic scaffolds to direct ordered or porous forms relevant to interfacial biomedical interactions ref [21].

From an application perspective, morphology is not merely descriptive: aspect ratio, surface roughness, porosity, and hierarchical organization govern protein adsorption, dissolution behavior, reactive oxygen species generation, and cell or microbial contact efficiency. Accordingly, controlling shape distributions in green ZnO synthesis is essential for translating eco-friendly fabrication into reproducible biomedical performance.

subsections.section_title: Green Synthesis Strategies and Design Parameters of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Scalability, reproducibility, and standardization challenges
subsections.content:
Despite the ecological appeal of plant- and microbe-mediated ZnO synthesis, translation from bench-scale batches to reliable production remains difficult. Biological extracts are intrinsically variable: species identity, cultivation conditions, harvest season, tissue age, extraction solvent, and storage history all alter the concentrations of polyphenols, sugars, proteins, and organic acids that act as reducing, complexing, and capping agents. Such compositional drift changes nucleation kinetics and growth pathways, leading to batch-to-batch variation in particle size, defect density, and surface chemistry. General analyses of green nanomanufacturing have therefore emphasized that sustainability claims must be coupled to process control, metrology, and life-cycle thinking rather than assuming that “bio-based” synthesis is automatically robust or scalable ref [6], ref [5].

For ZnO specifically, reproducibility is further complicated by the sensitivity of the wurtzite phase to pH, precursor hydrolysis rate, dissolved oxygen, calcination temperature, and post-synthesis washing, all of which can differ subtly across laboratories. Practical standardization should include reporting of extract preparation protocols, phytochemical or biomolecular fingerprints, Zn precursor purity, reactor geometry, mixing rate, aging time, and thermal history, alongside comparable characterization metrics such as hydrodynamic size, zeta potential, crystallite size, and surface-bound organics. Calls for such harmonized physicochemical characterization echo broader nano-EHS frameworks showing that variable ZnO properties strongly influence biological behavior and hazard profiles ref [2], ref [7].

Scalability also raises economic and regulatory questions. Continuous or semi-continuous reactors, in-line monitoring, and reference materials could reduce operator-dependent variability, but these approaches are still rarely implemented in green ZnO studies. More generally, safe-by-design thinking argues that manufacturability, reproducibility, and downstream safety assessment should be integrated early in nanomaterial development, particularly for biomedical ZnO where minor changes in surface corona or dissolution can alter efficacy and toxicity ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Structural and morphological characterization
subsections.content:
Structural and morphological characterization is the first step in relating green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials to biomedical performance. X-ray diffraction (XRD) is routinely used to verify phase-pure hexagonal wurtzite ZnO and to estimate crystallite size from line broadening, while electron microscopy resolves the particle architecture produced under biogenic growth conditions. ZnO is well known to form spheres, rods, flowers, sheets, and hierarchical aggregates depending on precursor chemistry and kinetic control during nucleation and growth ref [22], ref [1]. In green routes, these descriptors are especially important because phytochemicals or microbial metabolites often modulate anisotropic growth and defect formation relative to conventional precipitation or hydrothermal synthesis.

Scanning and transmission electron microscopies provide complementary information on particle size, aspect ratio, faceting, porosity, and degree of agglomeration; selected-area electron diffraction and high-resolution TEM further confirm crystallinity and lattice spacing. These nanoscale attributes are not merely descriptive: they govern accessible surface area, dissolution behavior, cellular internalization, and contact-dependent antimicrobial activity. For example, shape-dependent biointeractions of ZnO have been linked to differences in exposed crystal facets and reactive surface density, while smaller crystallites generally present higher surface reactivity and faster ion release ref [16], ref [2].

For green-synthesized systems, morphological interpretation should therefore integrate XRD with SEM/TEM and, where possible, dynamic light scattering or image-based size distributions, because dry-state primary dimensions can differ markedly from the agglomerated structures encountered in suspension. This multimodal characterization framework enables more reliable structure-property-bioactivity correlations and helps distinguish effects arising from intrinsic crystal structure from those caused by biogenic capping layers or aggregation state ref [1], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Surface chemistry and functional group analysis
subsections.content:
Surface chemistry is a critical determinant of how green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials behave in biological environments because the synthesis route leaves a molecular corona of plant-, algal-, or microbial-derived metabolites on the oxide surface. In practice, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) is most often used to identify residual hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxylate, amine, and phenolic groups, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) resolves their chemical states and the relative abundance of lattice oxygen, oxygen vacancies, and adsorbed oxygen species. For ZnO, the O 1s envelope is particularly informative because it can distinguish Zn–O lattice contributions from surface hydroxylation and defect-associated oxygen, features that are closely tied to colloidal behavior and interfacial reactivity ref [24], ref [25].

For biogenic ZnO, these surface functionalities are not merely synthesis residues; they can act as capping and stabilizing ligands that modulate crystal growth, reduce agglomeration, and alter surface charge. Phenolics, proteins, polysaccharides, and other biomolecules identified by FTIR or XPS can therefore influence protein adsorption, membrane interactions, dissolution kinetics, and reactive oxygen species generation under physiological conditions. This is consistent with broader analyses showing that surface defects and adsorbates strongly govern ZnO reactivity in aqueous and biological media ref [25], ref [10].

Correlating functional-group signatures with bioactivity is thus essential. A more hydroxylated or biomolecule-rich surface may improve dispersibility and biocompatibility, whereas higher densities of defect-associated oxygen sites can enhance photocatalytic and oxidative responses relevant to antimicrobial or anticancer action. Complementary use of FTIR, XPS, and zeta potential analysis is therefore especially important for distinguishing genuinely green surface passivation from bare or conventionally processed ZnO surfaces ref [24], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Optical and electronic properties
subsections.content:
Optical and electronic measurements are central to assessing how green synthesis modifies ZnO nanomaterials for biomedical use. UV–visible spectra typically show the characteristic near-band-edge absorption of ZnO, while shifts in the absorption edge reflect quantum-confinement effects, lattice strain, defect density, and biomolecule-mediated surface passivation. Photoluminescence (PL) is especially informative because the balance between ultraviolet excitonic emission and visible defect-related bands reports on oxygen vacancies, zinc interstitials, and surface states that govern charge separation and interfacial redox activity ref [1], ref [22].

These features are directly relevant to biological performance. Defect-rich ZnO generally exhibits stronger visible PL and enhanced reactive oxygen species generation under photoactivation, whereas improved crystallinity and reduced non-radiative recombination can favor more predictable optical readouts for imaging and sensing. The excitonic and defect emissions of ZnO nanostructures, together with their wide direct band gap and large exciton binding energy, underlie their utility in biosensors, fluorescence-based probes, and photocatalytically assisted antimicrobial systems ref [1], ref [14].

In green-synthesized ZnO, residual phytochemicals can further influence electronic structure by altering surface band bending, trap populations, and carrier transfer at the nano-bio interface. Such capping layers may suppress aggregation and tune surface defects, but they can also attenuate radiative emission or modify electron-transfer kinetics in physiological media. Correlating UV–vis, PL, and photoelectrochemical data with biological assays is therefore essential for linking synthesis-dependent electronic structure to antimicrobial efficacy, selective cytotoxicity, and diagnostic signal generation ref [22], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Colloidal stability and dispersibility in biological media
subsections.content:
Colloidal stability is a critical but often underreported determinant of the biomedical performance of green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials. In aqueous and physiological media, particle behavior is governed by the interplay of primary size, surface charge, adsorbed phytochemical corona, ionic strength, and protein binding. Standard descriptors such as hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity, and zeta potential therefore complement dry-state imaging, because ZnO frequently undergoes rapid agglomeration or sedimentation in cell culture media even when it appears well dispersed in water ref [26], ref [27].

For green ZnO, capping by plant-derived polyphenols, proteins, or polysaccharides can improve initial dispersibility through steric and electrosteric stabilization, but this effect is highly medium-dependent. In phosphate- and chloride-containing buffers, as well as serum-supplemented media, adsorption of biomolecules and partial dissolution can restructure the particle interface, shifting effective size and surface potential. Such transformations influence delivered dose, cellular uptake, and apparent toxicity, making dispersion protocol and exposure medium essential experimental variables rather than procedural details ref [27], ref [28].

Best practice therefore requires colloidal assessment in the exact biological medium used for testing, ideally over relevant time scales and with attention to dissolution. Dynamic light scattering, electrophoretic mobility measurements, and sedimentation-aware dosimetry are especially informative when interpreted alongside Zn2+ release, since particle settling and ion generation jointly shape antimicrobial and anticancer outcomes. Frameworks developed for nanotoxicology emphasize that reproducible bioactivity comparisons are not possible without concurrent characterization of agglomeration, stability, and medium-induced transformation ref [28], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Structure-property-bioactivity relationships
subsections.content:
Structure–property–bioactivity relationships in green-synthesized ZnO are governed by the coupled effects of size, shape, crystallinity, defect density, and the phytochemical corona inherited from biological reducing/capping agents. These parameters jointly control surface reactivity, Zn2+ release, colloidal behavior, and cellular interactions. More reactive facets and higher densities of oxygen-vacancy-related defects generally enhance reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, which can strengthen antimicrobial and anticancer activity but also increase nonspecific cytotoxicity, making bioactivity highly sensitive to synthesis-dependent structural heterogeneity ref [16], ref [2].

Particle morphology further modulates biological outcomes by altering membrane contact, internalization, and dissolution kinetics. Rods, wires, and flower-like assemblies often expose different crystal facets than near-spherical particles, leading to measurable differences in photocatalytic and biological performance. In microbial systems, ZnO activity has been linked to a combination of direct cell-envelope interaction, ROS production, and released zinc ions rather than any single mechanism alone ref [15]. For mammalian cells, nanoscale ZnO can trigger oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis, and these effects intensify as accessible surface area and defect-mediated redox activity increase ref [12].

For green ZnO specifically, residual plant- or microbe-derived surface ligands may attenuate aggregation, alter protein adsorption, and partially buffer acute toxicity while preserving therapeutic efficacy. This implies that identical nominal compositions can display different bioactivities depending on surface functionalization history. A key design principle is therefore to tune morphology and defect chemistry together with biogenic surface passivation to maximize selective antimicrobial or anticancer effects while minimizing off-target damage and improving translational reproducibility ref [2], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Structural Characterization and Functional Properties Relevant to Biomedicine
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative analysis of green versus conventionally synthesized ZnO
subsections.content:
Comparisons between green and conventionally synthesized ZnO consistently show that the synthesis route alters not only particle size and morphology, but also the surface state most relevant to biomedicine. Conventional precipitation, sol-gel, or hydrothermal routes often deliver better batch-to-batch control and higher crystallinity after calcination, whereas plant- or microbe-mediated routes frequently leave a corona of phytochemicals, proteins, or polysaccharides on the ZnO surface, creating distinct interfacial chemistry and colloidal behavior ref [17], ref [22]. This difference is important because biological identity is determined less by the crystal core alone than by the accessible surface presented in aqueous media.

From a functional perspective, green ZnO often exhibits enhanced dispersion stability, lower need for external capping agents, and in many reports stronger antimicrobial performance, which is commonly attributed to synergistic effects between ZnO and residual bioactive metabolites adsorbed during synthesis ref [19], ref [20]. By contrast, conventionally synthesized ZnO may provide cleaner model surfaces for mechanistic studies of dissolution, ROS generation, and defect-dependent optical responses, making it valuable when structure-property correlations must be isolated from organic surface contributions ref [25].

Thus, the comparison should not be framed simply as sustainability versus performance. Green routes may be advantageous for biocompatible surface functionalization and reduced reagent burden, but they also introduce variability in precursor composition and impurity profiles. Conventional routes remain preferable where crystallographic uniformity, defect engineering, and scalable process control are paramount. For biomedical translation, the critical issue is therefore standardization of post-synthesis purification and reporting, so that differences in bioactivity can be attributed to genuine materials design rather than uncontrolled synthetic residues.

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Antimicrobial and antibiofilm applications
subsections.content:
Green ZnO nanomaterials are widely investigated as broad-spectrum antimicrobials against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, with added relevance for biofilm-associated infections. Their activity is generally attributed to a combination of reactive oxygen species generation, membrane damage, surface contact effects, and Zn2+ release, while phytochemical capping agents introduced during green synthesis can modulate particle dispersion, interfacial adhesion, and bacterial interactions ref [10], ref [16]. These features are particularly attractive for eco-fabricated systems because residual plant- or microbe-derived metabolites may reduce the need for harsh stabilizers while preserving antimicrobial potency.

Beyond planktonic killing, ZnO nanostructures can interfere with early adhesion and mature biofilm integrity. Mechanistic studies on metal oxide nanoparticles have shown that ZnO suppresses foodborne and clinically relevant pathogens through oxidative stress and envelope disruption ref [16]. In parallel, biosynthesized ZnO nanoparticles prepared using Lactobacillus plantarum extracts displayed notable antibacterial efficacy and inhibited biofilm formation, supporting the view that biologically derived surface chemistries can enhance anti-adhesive and antibiofilm behavior ref [30]. Similar observations have been reported for plant-mediated ZnO nanoparticles synthesized from Calotropis gigantea leaf extract, which exhibited strong antibacterial activity against common pathogens ref [31].

From an application standpoint, these properties support the incorporation of green ZnO into wound dressings, coatings, and infection-resistant implant surfaces. Importantly, antibiofilm performance is often more clinically meaningful than minimum inhibitory concentration alone, because sessile communities are markedly more drug tolerant. Accordingly, future work should standardize comparisons across green synthetic routes, particle corona composition, and biofilm models to clarify when sustainability-driven synthesis also translates into superior antimicrobial function.

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Anticancer and tumor-targeted applications
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly investigated as anticancer agents because they couple the intrinsic cytotoxicity of ZnO with phytochemical capping layers that may improve colloidal stability and biological selectivity. A recurring mechanism is preferential uptake by tumor cells followed by intracellular Zn2+ release and reactive oxygen species generation, which disrupt mitochondrial function, damage DNA, and activate caspase-dependent apoptosis; these effects have been documented across multiple cancer models for ZnO nanoparticles more broadly, providing a mechanistic basis for evaluating eco-friendly variants in oncology ref [13], ref [12].

Tumor-targeted performance is also linked to physicochemical features shaped during green synthesis, including particle size, surface charge, and biomolecule corona composition. Plant- or microbe-derived surface ligands can modulate membrane interactions and may enhance differential toxicity toward malignant relative to nonmalignant cells, while the acidic tumor microenvironment can accelerate ZnO dissolution and amplify intracellular stress responses. In this context, selective cancer-cell killing and in vivo antitumor activity have been summarized in mechanistic reviews emphasizing oxidative stress, p53 signaling, and mitochondrial apoptosis as central pathways for ZnO-based systems ref [14].

Beyond direct cytotoxicity, green ZnO platforms are being explored as multifunctional carriers for chemotherapeutics and targeting ligands, where pH-responsive dissolution can support localized drug release in tumors. Such designs align well with theranostic strategies because ZnO can contribute both therapeutic action and imaging or sensing functionality. Although evidence remains uneven across formulations, current studies suggest that eco-friendly synthesis may reduce harmful residual reagents while preserving the pro-apoptotic and tumor-responsive behavior that underpins ZnO nanomedicine ref [14], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Drug delivery and controlled release systems
subsections.content:
Green ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly explored as drug-delivery carriers because they combine high surface reactivity, facile surface functionalization, and pH-responsive dissolution into Zn2+, which can accelerate cargo release in acidic endosomal or tumor-like microenvironments. This behavior is especially attractive for reducing premature leakage under physiological conditions while promoting intracellular unloading after uptake. In addition, the biogenic corona derived from plant or microbial synthesis can improve colloidal behavior and provide functional groups for conjugating drugs, polymers, or targeting ligands, thereby extending the utility of ZnO beyond a passive carrier platform ref [15], ref [29].

A representative strategy uses porous or core-shell ZnO architectures to enhance loading capacity and trigger release under acidic conditions. Hollow mesoporous ZnO nanocarriers have been shown to support high doxorubicin payloads and pH-dependent release, illustrating the suitability of ZnO frameworks for on-demand chemotherapy delivery ref [32]. Related work on biodegradable ZnO quantum dots has further demonstrated that nanoscale ZnO can serve simultaneously as an imaging-capable and pH-sensitive vehicle for intracellular drug transport, supporting its integration into multifunctional nanomedicine designs ref [33].

For green-synthesized ZnO specifically, the main translational advantage lies less in altering the basic dissolution mechanism than in reducing toxic synthetic residues and introducing naturally derived surface chemistries that may modulate loading, dispersibility, and biological interactions. Nonetheless, controlled release from biogenic ZnO remains sensitive to particle size, agglomeration state, and protein adsorption, all of which influence cellular uptake and effective intracellular dose; these parameters therefore require rigorous optimization when designing clinically relevant ZnO-based delivery systems ref [29], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Wound healing and tissue regeneration
subsections.content:
Green ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly explored for wound healing because they combine broad antimicrobial action with pro-regenerative functions relevant to re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, and angiogenic signaling. In tissue-engineering contexts, ZnO-containing scaffolds, fibers, and coatings can also improve surface bioactivity and cell–material interactions when Zn2+ release and particle loading are carefully controlled, helping to balance bactericidal efficacy with cytocompatibility ref [11], ref [34].

A recurrent design principle is incorporation of ZnO into biopolymeric wound dressings, where the inorganic phase provides antimicrobial protection while the matrix preserves moisture and structural support. Electrospun and hydrogel-like constructs containing ZnO have been reported to enhance fibroblast attachment and accelerate closure of infected or chronic wounds, effects often attributed to reduced microbial burden together with zinc-mediated support of keratinocyte and fibroblast functions ref [34], ref [35]. For green-synthesized ZnO in particular, phytochemical capping layers may further modulate interfacial interactions and lessen residual toxic contaminants from synthesis, which is advantageous for topical biomedical use ref [18].

Beyond soft-tissue repair, ZnO nanostructures have drawn attention in bone and broader tissue regeneration because their semiconducting, piezoelectric, and osteoconductive features can be coupled with polymeric or ceramic scaffolds to stimulate cell differentiation and matrix mineralization. Reviews of ZnO-based platforms therefore position them as multifunctional regenerative additives that can integrate infection control, bioactivity, and, in some architectures, mechanoelectrical stimulation within a single material system ref [11], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Bioimaging, sensing, and theranostic potential
subsections.content:
Green ZnO nanomaterials are attractive for bioimaging because ZnO is an intrinsically luminescent semiconductor whose defect- and exciton-mediated emission can be engineered through particle size, morphology, and surface chemistry. At the nanoscale, ZnO has been explored for optical imaging, while its comparatively low cost and biodegradability into Zn2+ provide advantages over some heavy-metal-based probes. Early demonstrations of multifunctional ZnO nanostructures for imaging and therapy, including pH-responsive platforms, helped establish ZnO as a candidate theranostic material rather than a purely structural oxide ref [36].

In biosensing, ZnO offers a high isoelectric point, large surface area, and favorable electron-transfer characteristics, enabling immobilization of enzymes, antibodies, and nucleic acids on nanorods, nanowires, and porous particles. These properties have supported electrochemical and optical sensing of glucose, cholesterol, and other biomolecules, as summarized in foundational reviews of ZnO nanostructures for biosensor design ref [37], ref [38]. For green-synthesized ZnO, phytochemical capping layers may further modulate colloidal stability and biorecognition interfaces, although batch-to-batch variability in surface corona formation remains a practical limitation for translational sensor reproducibility.

Theranostically, ZnO is especially interesting because the same platform can combine fluorescence, stimulus-responsive dissolution, and drug loading. pH-sensitive degradation in acidic intracellular or tumor-like microenvironments can promote image-guided release of payloads while simultaneously enhancing cytotoxic or antimicrobial action through Zn2+ liberation and reactive oxygen species generation ref [36], ref [39]. Recent reviews of ZnO quantum dots and related nanostructures also highlight opportunities for multimodal imaging, biosensing, and combined diagnosis-treatment systems, but emphasize that surface passivation, emission stability in biological fluids, and in vivo safety profiling remain key barriers to clinical adoption ref [39], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Biomedical Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant-related biomedical roles
subsections.content:
Beyond direct antimicrobial or cytotoxic actions, green ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly investigated as modulators of oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling. Their biomedical relevance is nuanced: ZnO can either generate reactive oxygen species at high dose or, when appropriately engineered and administered at biocompatible levels, attenuate inflammation by supplying bioavailable Zn2+, altering redox balance, and suppressing pro-inflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, COX-2, and NF-kappaB-associated pathways ref [41], ref [42]. This dual behavior makes synthesis route, surface phytochemistry, particle size, and dose especially important in anti-inflammatory design.

Evidence from green synthesis studies indicates that plant-capped ZnO nanoparticles may show enhanced radical-scavenging and membrane-protective behavior relative to conventionally prepared counterparts, likely because residual phenolics, flavonoids, or other phytoconstituents remain associated with the particle surface. For example, biosynthesized ZnO systems have repeatedly shown measurable DPPH or related antioxidant activity alongside acceptable cytocompatibility, supporting their use in inflammation-linked wound environments and oxidative-stress-associated tissue injury ref [43], ref [44]. In parallel, zinc itself is a recognized immunomodulatory micronutrient, and zinc deficiency is closely linked to exaggerated inflammatory responses and impaired antioxidant defense ref [45].

For translational use, however, anti-inflammatory benefit must be balanced against the well-documented capacity of ZnO nanoparticles to trigger oxidative injury under unfavorable exposure conditions. Accordingly, future work should distinguish protective redox modulation from nonspecific ROS induction through standardized dosing, corona-aware characterization, and in vivo validation in chronic inflammatory models. Within such a framework, green ZnO nanomaterials are best viewed as context-dependent nano-bioactive platforms whose anti-inflammatory and antioxidant functions derive from the combined effects of the ZnO core and the biomolecular shell generated during eco-friendly synthesis ref [41], ref [42], ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: Cellular uptake and intracellular fate
subsections.content:
Cellular uptake of ZnO nanomaterials is governed by the delivered dose at the cell surface, hydrodynamic size, aggregation state, and the protein corona formed in biological media. For ZnO systems, these parameters strongly influence sedimentation and diffusion, which in turn alter the effective cellular exposure and apparent uptake kinetics; this is particularly important when comparing green-synthesized particles whose phytochemical capping layers can change colloidal behavior relative to uncapped materials ref [27]. More generally, nanoparticle size and surface chemistry modulate serum protein adsorption and macrophage internalization, providing a useful framework for understanding why biosynthesized ZnO often shows cell-type-specific uptake patterns ref [29].

After association with the plasma membrane, ZnO nanoparticles are commonly internalized through energy-dependent endocytic pathways and trafficked to endosomes and lysosomes, where acidic pH promotes partial dissolution and intracellular Zn2+ release. This 'Trojan horse' behavior has been described as a central determinant of ZnO bioreactivity, linking uptake to oxidative stress, organelle injury, and downstream signaling responses ref [2]. In mammalian cells, dissolution in lysosomal compartments can amplify local zinc concentrations beyond homeostatic buffering capacity, thereby perturbing mitochondrial function and redox balance ref [10].

For green-synthesized ZnO, intracellular fate may further depend on the persistence of adsorbed plant- or microbe-derived metabolites, which can alter membrane interactions, vesicular processing, and dissolution kinetics. Accordingly, mechanistic uptake studies should report not only nominal particle dimensions but also corona composition, dispersion stability, and intracellular zinc speciation, since these factors help distinguish particle-specific trafficking from responses driven predominantly by released ions ref [2], ref [10], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanisms of biological activity
subsections.content:
The biological activity of ZnO nanomaterials is generally attributed to a combination of particle-specific and ion-mediated processes rather than a single dominant mechanism. A central pathway is oxidative stress: ZnO can promote intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, disrupt mitochondrial membrane potential, and activate apoptotic signaling cascades. In mammalian cells, these events have been linked to oxidative DNA damage, cytochrome c release, caspase activation, and mitochondrial dysfunction, indicating that redox imbalance is a key mechanistic hub for both therapeutic and toxic effects ref [12].

A second major mechanism is the progressive dissolution of ZnO and the consequent elevation of bioavailable Zn2+, particularly in acidic intracellular compartments such as endosomes and lysosomes. This “Trojan horse” behavior can disturb zinc homeostasis, impair enzyme function, alter membrane integrity, and amplify oxidative and proteotoxic stress. Mechanistic analyses have shown that the relative contributions of particle surface reactivity and released ions depend strongly on medium composition, pH, and exposure conditions, which is highly relevant when interpreting the behavior of green-synthesized ZnO carrying plant- or microbe-derived surface coronas ref [46], ref [47].

For antimicrobial action, ZnO is understood to act through overlapping mechanisms including ROS generation, Zn2+ release, and direct damage to bacterial envelopes, leading to permeability loss, metabolic inhibition, and cell death ref [16]. In cancer models, these same pathways may be accentuated by the higher basal oxidative stress and altered membrane trafficking of tumor cells, helping explain reports of selective cytotoxicity under some conditions ref [13]. For green ZnO systems, phytochemical capping agents may further modulate these mechanisms by changing dissolution kinetics, colloidal stability, protein adsorption, and interactions with cellular redox pathways.

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: In vitro cytotoxicity and biocompatibility assessment
subsections.content:
In vitro cytotoxicity assessment of green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials should move beyond single end-point viability assays to a panel that captures metabolic activity, membrane integrity, oxidative stress, and cell death mode. Across mammalian models, ZnO nanoparticles can interfere with colorimetric readouts and sediment rapidly, making delivered dose, dispersion state, and assay orthogonality critical for interpretation ref [48], ref [28]. For green systems, these issues are compounded by phytochemical or biomolecular capping layers, which may either attenuate acute toxicity by limiting dissolution and protein adsorption or introduce batch-dependent variability if residual extract components are not adequately controlled.

A recurring observation is that ZnO exhibits cell-type-dependent toxicity, with transformed cells often showing greater susceptibility than normal cells, a pattern linked to differential redox balance, membrane trafficking, and sensitivity to Zn2+-associated stress. In a comparative in vitro analysis, Sharma et al. reported selective killing of cancer cells by ZnO nanoparticles relative to normal cells, supporting the idea that biocompatibility cannot be generalized across target tissues ref [49]. Likewise, Hanley et al. showed that both particle size and cellular context shape ZnO cytotoxicity profiles, emphasizing the need to benchmark green ZnO against conventional materials of matched dimensions and surface charge ref [50].

For biomedical screening, biocompatibility claims are strongest when viability data are complemented by hemolysis-compatible media studies, long-term proliferation or clonogenic assays, and mechanistic indicators such as ROS generation, mitochondrial depolarization, and intracellular zinc release. Standardized in vitro dosimetry frameworks are especially important because agglomeration and sedimentation can cause nominal concentration to substantially overestimate or underestimate true cellular exposure ref [28], ref [27]. Accordingly, rigorous assessment of green ZnO should integrate physicochemical characterization in culture media with multiple relevant cell models, including primary cells whenever feasible.

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: Hemocompatibility, immunological effects, and inflammation
subsections.content:
For biomedical deployment, hemocompatibility is a primary gatekeeping criterion because ZnO nanomaterials may contact blood directly or indirectly after administration. Reported blood-related effects of ZnO nanoparticles include erythrocyte membrane damage, hemolysis, platelet perturbation, and activation of coagulation or complement pathways, with severity strongly influenced by particle size, surface chemistry, agglomeration, and dissolution behavior ref [51], ref [52]. In green-synthesized systems, phytochemical capping layers can either mitigate these interactions by reducing direct membrane contact and limiting protein adsorption, or introduce batch-dependent variability if residual biomolecules alter colloidal stability in plasma.

Immunologically, ZnO nanoparticles are recognized as redox-active materials that can trigger innate immune signaling in phagocytic cells. Macrophage and monocyte studies consistently link ZnO exposure to ROS generation, lysosomal destabilization, Zn2+ release, and downstream induction of pro-inflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8; these responses often increase with smaller particle size and higher effective dose ref [50], ref [53]. Beyond soluble-ion effects alone, particle internalization and endo-lysosomal processing appear central to cytokine production, indicating that immune activation depends on both nanomaterial identity and biotransformation kinetics.

Inflammatory consequences observed in vivo are broadly consistent with these in vitro findings. Pulmonary exposure studies have shown neutrophilic inflammation and acute phase responses after ZnO nanoparticle inhalation or instillation, supporting a mechanism in which epithelial injury, oxidative stress, and leukocyte recruitment amplify tissue-level toxicity ref [54]. For green ZnO formulations, hemocompatibility and immunotoxicity therefore require explicit testing in protein-containing media and whole-blood or primary immune-cell models, since synthesis route alone does not guarantee reduced inflammatory hazard.

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: In vivo toxicity, biodistribution, and clearance
subsections.content:
In vivo studies indicate that ZnO nanomaterials can produce organ- and route-dependent toxicological responses, with the lung, liver, kidney, and spleen emerging as frequent targets. Inhalation exposure is particularly informative for hazard identification: acute pulmonary exposure to nano-ZnO in mice caused marked inflammation and injury, consistent with the high solubility/reactivity of ZnO in biological milieus and the contribution of released Zn2+ to tissue damage ref [54]. Systemic administration studies likewise show that toxicity is strongly dose dependent and often amplified by smaller particle size, higher surface area, and faster dissolution kinetics.

Biodistribution after parenteral exposure generally follows reticuloendothelial sequestration, with preferential accumulation in the liver and spleen and, to a lesser extent, kidney and lung. In mice, Wang et al. reported size-dependent biodistribution and acute toxicity of intravenously administered ZnO nanoparticles, with nanoforms producing greater tissue accumulation and more pronounced pathological changes than larger particles ref [55]. These patterns are broadly consistent with classic nanotoxicology principles in which hydrodynamic size, aggregation state, and surface corona regulate vascular residence and mononuclear phagocyte uptake.

Clearance of ZnO differs from that of poorly soluble metal oxides because dissolution is often a major elimination pathway. ZnO can transform in vivo into ionic zinc and zinc-containing complexes, enabling partial renal and hepatobiliary elimination, but also complicating interpretation because measured tissue zinc reflects both particles and dissolved species. Long et al. showed that pulmonary responses to ZnO nanoparticles were closely linked to particle solubility and zinc ion bioavailability ref [56], while Cho et al. demonstrated substantial acute systemic toxicity and tissue injury after repeated oral dosing in rats ref [57]. For green-synthesized ZnO systems, these findings imply that any reduction in in vivo hazard must be demonstrated experimentally rather than assumed from the plant- or microbe-derived route, with special attention to dissolution rate, residual phytochemicals, and colloidal stability under physiological conditions.

subsections.section_title: Biological Interactions, Safety, and Mechanistic Insights
subsections.subsection_title: Determinants of safety in green-synthesized systems
subsections.content:
In green-synthesized ZnO systems, safety is determined not only by the ZnO core but also by the synthetic corona inherited from plant, algal, or microbial extracts. This bioorganic layer can alter hydrodynamic size, agglomeration, surface charge, and protein adsorption, thereby changing sedimentation, cellular contact, and immune recognition relative to conventionally prepared particles. More broadly, nanoparticle uptake and biological reactivity are strongly conditioned by agglomeration state and surface chemistry, while adsorption of biomolecules at the nano–bio interface critically shapes biodistribution and biocompatibility ref [27], ref [52].

A second determinant is dissolution behavior. For ZnO, many adverse effects track the kinetics of Zn2+ release, which depend on particle size, defect structure, medium composition, and the presence of capping phytochemicals or microbial metabolites. Evidence from comparative toxicology has shown that solubility is a major driver of ZnO hazard, sometimes outweighing nominal particle identity itself ref [46]. In green routes, incomplete purification may further leave residual reductants, phenolics, proteins, or salts that either mitigate toxicity through passivation and antioxidant effects or increase variability and off-target responses.

Accordingly, safer-by-design green ZnO requires attention to precursor purity, reproducible extract composition, washing and calcination history, colloidal stability in relevant biological media, and delivered rather than administered dose. These principles are consistent with broader safe-by-design frameworks in nanotechnology, which emphasize integrating functionality, exposure control, and hazard reduction from the earliest stages of material development ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Standardization of green synthesis and characterization protocols
subsections.content:
A major translational barrier for green ZnO nanomaterials is the poor reproducibility of synthesis routes that rely on biologically complex reducing and capping systems. Plant extracts, microbial supernatants, and biopolymer matrices vary with species, growth conditions, harvest season, extraction solvent, pH, and storage history, making cross-study comparison difficult even when nominally similar protocols are reported. More standardized reporting is therefore needed for precursor concentration, extract composition or at least extraction ratio, reaction temperature-time profile, mixing order, and post-synthesis purification, consistent with broader green nanotechnology and biosynthesis literature ref [17], ref [6].

Standardization must also extend beyond synthetic inputs to a core characterization panel. For biomedical use, reporting only UV-Vis spectra and TEM images is insufficient; minimally, studies should quantify primary size and morphology, hydrodynamic size in relevant media, zeta potential, crystallinity, surface chemistry, impurity burden, dissolution behavior, and colloidal stability after sterilization and protein exposure. The need for harmonized dispersion and pre-exposure characterization has been emphasized in nanotoxicology methodology, because biological responses can shift substantially with aggregation state and medium composition rather than nominal particle size alone ref [26], ref [28].

For green ZnO specifically, protocol harmonization should include reference materials and interlaboratory benchmarking to distinguish effects caused by ZnO itself from those caused by residual phytochemicals or batch-specific corona formation. Adopting checklist-based reporting frameworks and safe-by-design thinking at the development stage would improve comparability, support quality-by-design manufacturing, and facilitate eventual regulatory assessment of green formulations intended for antimicrobial, wound-healing, or drug-delivery applications ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Batch consistency, quality control, and manufacturing translation
subsections.content:
A major translational barrier for green ZnO nanomaterials is batch-to-batch variability arising from the intrinsic heterogeneity of biological reducing and capping agents. Plant extracts and microbial supernatants vary with species, growth conditions, harvest season, extraction solvent, and storage history, which can alter ZnO nucleation kinetics, impurity profiles, surface chemistry, and ultimately biological performance. This problem is amplified for biomedical use, where small changes in size distribution, agglomeration state, dissolution behavior, or residual biomolecule content may shift antimicrobial efficacy, cytotoxicity, and biodistribution [1,2].

Accordingly, manufacturing translation requires quality systems that extend beyond simple confirmation of particle formation. Critical quality attributes should include particle size and polydispersity, crystal phase, zeta potential, colloidal stability in relevant media, endotoxin/bioburden status, residual precursor and solvent levels, and Zn2+ release under physiological conditions. The need to link physicochemical attributes to biological response is consistent with broader nanomedicine development principles, including rigorous characterization, scalable process control, and reproducible material identity across lots [3,4]. For green routes, this also implies standardizing the biological feedstock itself through authenticated source material, predefined extraction procedures, and in-process controls.

From a manufacturing perspective, proof-of-concept flask synthesis must evolve toward GMP-compatible, scalable, and contamination-controlled production. Continuous or semi-continuous synthesis, process analytical technologies, and design-of-experiments optimization may help reduce lot variability, but these strategies remain underused for green ZnO systems. More broadly, successful translation of nanomaterials has shown that early attention to manufacturability, sterility assurance, storage stability, and validated release specifications is essential if promising laboratory formulations are to become clinically reliable products [4,5].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Regulatory and ethical considerations in biomedical nanotechnology
subsections.content:
Regulatory translation of green ZnO nanomaterials is complicated by the fact that “green” synthesis does not automatically imply safety, quality, or regulatory acceptability. For biomedical products, regulators increasingly expect a life-cycle perspective in which material identity, impurity profile, degradation behavior, and exposure route are all linked to risk assessment rather than inferred from the use of botanical or microbial feedstocks alone. This is especially important for ZnO systems, whose biological effects can depend on dissolution, ion release, corona formation, and dose metric, raising challenges for classification and hazard evaluation under conventional chemical and device frameworks ref [47], ref [61].

A central ethical and governance issue is how to operationalize safe-by-design principles without slowing innovation. Design choices such as precursor selection, residual biogenic constituents, surface coatings, and intended route of administration should be justified not only for efficacy but also for reproducibility, worker safety, environmental release, and end-of-life disposal. Responsible development therefore requires transparency in sourcing biological materials, traceability of manufacturing steps, and early integration of safety testing that is proportionate to realistic exposure scenarios ref [8], ref [7].

For clinical translation, preclinical evidence must also satisfy ethical expectations around relevance and robustness. Poorly characterized formulations, nonstandard dosing, and limited comparability across models undermine both animal welfare and regulatory confidence. Future guidance for green ZnO nanomedicine will likely need harmonized reporting standards, clearer criteria for nano-specific benefit-risk assessment, and attention to informed consent and equity when nanoplatforms incorporate personalized or biologically derived components ref [61], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Limitations in preclinical evidence and model selection
subsections.content:
A major barrier to translating green ZnO nanomaterials is that preclinical evidence remains fragmented, with heavy reliance on short-term in vitro cytotoxicity studies using a small number of immortalized cell lines. Such models rarely capture realistic exposure conditions, particle transformation in biological media, or delivered dose at the cell surface, all of which can strongly alter apparent toxicity and therapeutic index. Sedimentation, agglomeration, and medium-dependent dissolution are especially important for ZnO systems and can confound comparisons across studies if dosimetry is not standardized ref [28], ref [27].

Model selection is also frequently poorly aligned with the intended biomedical application. For example, antimicrobial or anticancer claims are often based on simplified monoculture assays, whereas clinically relevant performance depends on interactions with immune cells, extracellular matrices, blood proteins, and organ-specific barriers. Protein corona formation and macrophage uptake can substantially redirect biodistribution and cellular responses, implying that serum composition, cell type, and exposure route should be treated as experimental variables rather than background conditions ref [29].

In vivo evidence is comparatively limited and often restricted to acute toxicity endpoints, making it difficult to infer chronic safety, clearance, reproductive risk, or immunological consequences. Studies of inhalation and oral exposure to ZnO nanoparticles in rodents have shown that organ-level responses can differ markedly from in vitro predictions, underscoring the need for route-specific animal models, longer follow-up, and benchmark comparisons against conventionally synthesized ZnO and soluble zinc salts ref [54], ref [57]. Future preclinical pipelines should therefore integrate standardized dispersion/dosimetry methods, advanced co-culture or organotypic systems, and hypothesis-driven in vivo validation.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Advanced functionalization and hybrid green ZnO systems
subsections.content:
Advanced functionalization is a key route for overcoming the intrinsic limitations of green-synthesized ZnO, particularly colloidal instability, burst dissolution, and insufficient selectivity in complex biological environments. Surface engineering with polymers, biomolecules, or targeting ligands can modulate protein adsorption, cellular uptake, and drug-loading behavior, while preserving the sustainability advantages of biosynthetic routes. In parallel, hollow or porous ZnO architectures provide higher payload capacity and pH-responsive release, which is especially relevant for antimicrobial delivery and cancer theranostics ref [32], ref [40].

Hybrid green ZnO systems are also increasingly attractive because they decouple core functionality from biological interface design. Composites incorporating ZnO with biopolymers, electrospun matrices, or other inorganic domains can improve mechanical robustness, reduce aggregation, and introduce multimodal functions such as imaging, sensing, or combination therapy. Recent reviews of ZnO nanomaterials and nanocomposites emphasize that hybridization is central to next-generation theranostic platforms, but also note that interface chemistry, shell uniformity, and degradation kinetics remain insufficiently standardized for biomedical translation ref [39], ref [35].

For future development, the major challenge is not simply adding more components, but designing functionalized green ZnO systems with reproducible structure-property relationships and clinically relevant performance. Priorities include ligand density control, corona-aware targeting strategies, and scalable biofabrication workflows that maintain batch consistency after conjugation or encapsulation. These issues will determine whether hybrid green ZnO platforms can progress from promising multifunctional prototypes to robust precision nanomedicine tools ref [39], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Toward personalized and precision nanomedicine
subsections.content:
Moving green ZnO nanomaterials toward personalized and precision nanomedicine requires a shift from largely generic formulations to systems designed around inter-patient variability in tumor biology, immune status, route-specific exposure, and zinc homeostasis. More broadly, clinical translation of nanomedicines has shown that heterogeneity in vascular permeability, mononuclear phagocyte system activity, and biomarker expression can strongly alter efficacy and safety, implying that green ZnO platforms will likely need patient-stratified rather than one-size-fits-all development pathways ref [60], ref [59].

For ZnO specifically, precision design is plausible because their therapeutic behavior depends on pH-responsive dissolution, reactive oxygen species generation, and surface-mediated interactions, all of which are influenced by disease microenvironment and host biology. Experimental studies showing selective oxidative stress and apoptosis in cancer cells suggest that ZnO systems may be most effective when matched to tumors with exploitable redox imbalance or acidic intracellular compartments ref [49], while molecular analyses of selective cancer targeting indicate that uptake and cytotoxicity vary across cell types and in vivo settings ref [13]. In parallel, personalized use will require accounting for the patient-specific protein corona, since plasma protein adsorption can reshape biodistribution, cellular uptake, and therapeutic performance after administration ref [52].

Future precision strategies should therefore integrate green synthesis with biomarker-guided functionalization, ex vivo profiling in patient-derived organoids or immune co-cultures, and adaptive dosing frameworks linked to dissolution and pharmacodynamic readouts. Such an approach could help identify the subsets of patients most likely to benefit from ZnO-based antimicrobial, anticancer, or wound-healing interventions while reducing off-target toxicity and improving regulatory acceptability.
